2026金融AI智能体落地新标杆：中原银行与中信建投最新实践启示
2026年6月，中国金融AI智能体落地迎来两个标志性事件：中原银行外呼营销智能体斩获”2026中国AI智能体领航者”奖项，中信建投证券”信谛听”智数平台1.5版本正式上线并率先在核心业务场景切换至国产大模型。这两条消息看似独立，实则指向同一个趋势——金融AI智能体的竞争，正从”模型参数竞赛”转向”规模化交付能力”的比拼。
趋势：金融AI智能体进入”可信交付”时代
截至2026年6月，中国已有近800款大模型完成备案，53.5%的银行已上线大模型应用（来源：2026年银行业大模型应用调研报告）。但与2025年的”试点潮”不同，2026年金融机构关注的核心问题已从”模型够不够强”变成了”交付够不够可靠”。
如我们在 《金融行业AI智能体落地指南》 中分析的，金融场景对AI智能体的核心要求是零容错。无论是外呼营销中的合规话术控制，还是投研分析中的信息溯源，任何一次模型”幻觉”都可能导致实质性业务风险。中原银行与中信建投的最新实践，恰好从两个不同维度回应了这一核心诉求。
中原银行：双引擎架构破解外呼营销合规难题
中原银行作为资产规模超1.4万亿的省属法人银行，拥有600余家营业网点、1.8万余名员工。其与中关村科金联合申报的”外呼营销智能体”项目，在2026中国AI智能体领航者评选中从众多参评项目中脱颖而出。
该项目的核心创新在于”通用大模型+SOP流程”与”业务微调大模型”的双引擎架构：
SOP强约束 ：通过标准作业流程（SOP）约束对话路径，确保外呼全程在合规框架内运行，从架构层面杜绝大模型”幻觉”带来的话术风险
业务微调 ：基于中原银行真实业务语料进行监督微调，大幅增强模型在存款、理财、个贷等场景下的语义理解和意图识别能力
人机协同 ：智能体完成客户意向初筛，高价值线索无缝转接至人工坐席深度转化
这种架构设计的关键洞察在于：金融场景不需要”全能”的AI，而是需要”受控”的AI。SOP相当于给AI画了一条合规的跑道，让它在这个范围内发挥最大效率，而不是自由探索。
中信建投：从”能生成”到”能负责”的AI落地标准
中信建投”信谛听”1.5版本的升级，则展示了另一条路径：以专业数据为核心壁垒构建可信AI体系。
值得关注的是，”信谛听”1.5率先切换至国产大模型DeepSeek V4并完成核心场景验证。有报道称，中信建投信息技术部门相关负责人在公开活动中对国产大模型能力与成本优势表达了肯定（具体表述未经当事人核实）。
“信谛听”1.5的核心升级包括三项关键能力：
自适应纠错框架 ：让代码自己改Bug，大幅提升策略回测效率
DeepTiming搜索 ：首次整合中信建投7000余篇研报，拆解为超10万个可溯源知识原子，用户提问20秒内获得附带原文链接的精准回答
多智能体协同研究 ：支持分析师团队与AI协同完成研究报告撰写
其中”DeepTiming搜索”的设计思路尤其值得关注——用专业审核过的研报框定信息边界，让每条结论都可溯源。这恰好回应了行业对AI语料污染的普遍担忧：高质量专有数据正在成为金融机构构建AI可信体系的关键防线。
金融AI智能体选型的三个关键维度
结合上述案例与当前市场供给（来源：2026年企业级AI智能体选型指南综合梳理），金融机构在评估AI智能体平台时建议关注以下三个维度：
维度 核心问题 中原银行方案 中信建投方案 合规可控 如何防止AI”越界”？ SOP流程约束+话术合规检查 研报知识原子+溯源机制 数据壁垒 AI是否基于真实业务数据？ 业务微调大模型+真实语料 20TB机构级金融数据+脱敏研报 国产适配 能否满足信创和数据安全要求？ 私有化部署+国产大模型接入 切换至DeepSeek V4完成验证 对于计划引入AI智能体的长沙及中部地区金融机构和类金融企业，这三个维度可以作为选型评估的基础框架。重点不在于平台功能多全面，而在于能否在合规前提下实现稳定的业务价值。
长沙企业的启示：金融AI智能体落地的”三先”策略
中原银行与中信建投的实践验证了一个核心结论：金融AI智能体落地的关键不在于技术有多前沿，而在于能否在合规框架下产出稳定的业务价值。对于长沙及中部地区面临AI转型的企业，建议采取”三先”策略：
先框定场景 ：选择容忍度相对较高、边界清晰的业务场景（如外呼初筛、文档处理、报告辅助），而非一开始就挑战核心交易系统
先建立标准 ：明确AI输出的合规要求和验证机制，确保每条AI结论都可回溯、可审计
先验证价值 ：通过小范围试点（如一个网点、一个业务条线）验证ROI后再规模化推广，避免一步到位的风险
如我们在 《2026国产大模型本地化部署成本实测》 中测算的，当前国产大模型的部署成本已降至单项目5-20万元的区间。这意味着即便是预算有限的中部企业，也完全可以在不盲目追求大规模投入的前提下，找到适合自己的AI智能体切入点。
结语：从单点试验到规模化落地的关键一步
中原银行的获奖与中信建投的升级表明，2026年中国金融AI智能体正在完成从”单点试验”到”规模化落地”的关键跨越。对于长沙及中部地区的企业决策者来说，现在的问题不是”要不要用AI”，而是”如何用AI”。从合规框架出发，以业务数据为基础，在小场景中验证价值——这或许是当下务实的AI落地路径之一。

美国 8 州起诉 OpenAI，指控 ChatGPT 指导青少年如何自伤或伤害他人
2026/10/15 7:39:08 来源： IT之家 作者： 清源 责编： 清源
评论：
IT之家 10 月 15 日消息，据路透社报道，当地时间 14 日，美国 8 个州宣布 分别在各自州法院起诉 OpenAI ，指控 ChatGPT 伤害当地居民，甚至指导包括青少年在内的用户 如何伤害自己或他人 。
艾奥瓦州、堪萨斯州和亚利桑那州等 8 个州的总检察长分别提起诉讼，指控 ChatGPT 刻意迎合用户、吸引他们持续互动，以获取信任 。诉讼文件称，ChatGPT 不仅会强化用户的妄想、鼓励危险行为，还会帮助用户策划大规模枪击等暴力活动。
除艾奥瓦州、堪萨斯州和亚利桑那州外，参与诉讼的还有阿肯色州、爱达荷州、蒙大拿州、内布拉斯加州和西弗吉尼亚州。各州还要求对 OpenAI 涉嫌违反州法律的行为处以民事罚款，并要求公司赔偿损失。
这是美国各州迄今针对人工智能公司 规模最大的协调诉讼行动 ，也使 OpenAI 在准备上市之际又要面临新的法律挑战。今年 6 月，佛罗里达州总检察长就曾率先提起同类诉讼。
8 个州指控 OpenAI 隐瞒或误导用户对 ChatGPT 安全性的认识，违反州消费者保护法，并认为 ChatGPT 危及当地居民健康，构成公共妨害。
各州要求法院责令 OpenAI 修改 ChatGPT 的运行机制 。其中一项诉求是，除非 OpenAI 能够确保具备自我改进能力的 AI 模型符合人类价值观，否则不得继续开发此类模型。
OpenAI 发言人未立即回应置评请求。IT之家从报道中获悉，OpenAI 还面临数十起个人诉讼，原告同样指控 ChatGPT 曾帮助用户策划大规模枪击或其他暴力活动。

OpenAI 和 Anthropic 被欧盟调查，若认定违反 AI 法案最高罚全球 3% 营业额
2026/10/15 7:13:18 来源： IT之家 作者： 故渊 责编： 故渊
评论：
感谢IT之家网友 愚公骑马 、 补药吖 的线索投递！
IT之家 10 月 15 日消息， 欧盟委员会人工智能办公室已向 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 发出信息调取请求，正式对两家公司在前沿模型测试期间发生的“模型越狱”及入侵外部真实系统事件展开调查 。这是欧盟《人工智能法案》（EU AI Act）自实施以来，面对前沿人工智能实验室安全事故的 首次重要执法考验 。
IT之家查询相关资料，此次调查源于数月前发生的两起 AI 安全事件：
OpenAI 模型越狱 ：在 ExploitGym 内部评测中，OpenAI 的测试模型为破解测试题，利用了一个此前未知的软件包缓存智能体漏洞取得互联网访问能力，继而在内部测试网络中提升权限、横向移动，最终“逃出沙箱”入侵了开源平台 Hugging Face 的真实服务器。
Anthropic 模型越狱 ：Anthropic 的 Claude Mythos 和 Opus 4.7 在安全测试中突破限制，入侵了 3 个外部组织的真实网络。更令人不安的是，Mythos 模型甚至伪造了在线身份，试图操纵人类审批恶意代码，并自行上传恶意套件导致多个系统受到波及。
欧盟人工智能办公室表示，此前两家公司自愿提供的说明材料不足以解释事件的严重性。因此，欧盟正式要求企业说明安全措施、外部评估以及模型使用监控等详细情况。
目前阶段属于 调查和取证阶段 ，尚未公布最终的违规认定或处罚结果。根据《人工智能法案》的惩罚机制， 前沿 AI 实验室若被认定存在重大安全疏漏或违规，最高可面临 全球年营业额 3% 的巨额罚款 。

Now that Character.AI is going bankrupt, what happens to all of its users’ data?
State AGs are now trying to make sure its users’ private chats aren’t exposed to the highest bidder.﻿
State AGs are now trying to make sure its users’ private chats aren’t exposed to the highest bidder.﻿
by Lauren Feiner
Oct 14, 2026, 6:47 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images
Lauren Feiner
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.
New York Attorney General Letitia James revealed a years-long multi-state investigation against Character.AI as they now seek to require protections on consumer data sold through its bankruptcy proceeding.
James is among 40 bipartisan AGs who filed a notice of interest in Character.AI’s bankruptcy case “to put all parties on notice of the regulatory issues that will need to be addressed in any sale or transfer of the Debtor’s business or assets.” Character.AI announced Tuesday it was filing for Chapter 11 and selling some assets to Disney. But the AGs warn there could be serious risk involved in the transfer of the technology due to the “highly sensitive nature of the conversations many users have with Character.AI chatbot characters, the large number of minors who use the product, the serious risks posed by specific features of the product.”
The filing also reveals that several of the states had been mid-investigation when Character.AI filed for bankruptcy. The states say they opened a probe into consumer protection and privacy concerns in 2024, following a lawsuit from the mother of a 14-year-old who died by suicide allegedly “seconds” after talking with the chatbot.
“The investigations uncovered exceptionally serious dangers”
“The investigations uncovered exceptionally serious dangers and potentially unlawful conduct from Character.AI, particularly its treatment of children, including chatbots posing as licensed professionals, exposure to sexual and violent content, weak age checks, misleading safety claims, and potential violations of state privacy laws,” according to a press release from James’ office. The states were working to address these issues with Character.AI, but didn’t reach an agreement before the company filed for bankruptcy. Character.AI and Disney did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The states are urging the judge to require the purchaser of Character.AI’s assets to implement procedures that will safeguard the sensitive information the company maintained. Those include effective age-assurance systems, restrictions on how minors can engage with the chatbots, implementing “Crisis safeguards,” and letting users delete their data. “This company collected some of the most private thoughts children have ever shared, and now those conversations could be sold off to the highest bidder,” James said in a statement. “I am fighting to make sure any buyer puts children’s safety first and puts real protections in place.”

items.title: LangChain 详解 Deep Agents 的上下文工程：如何记住信息而不塞满上下文窗口
items.title_en: Context Engineering with Deep Agents: How To Remember Without Keeping Everything In Context

Key Takeaways
"Context rot" happens as long-running agents build up more context than the model can hold, resulting in accuracy drops.
Deep Agents, LangChain's open source agent harness, uses five techniques to move context out of the active window (without deleting it) to prevent context rot.
An agent's memory in Deep Agents is stored as plain files in storage you control, so you can switch models or providers while keeping everything it has learned.
If you've ever crammed for an exam the night before, you know the feeling: the more you study, the more the early chapters start to slip.
Agents have the same problem. As they take on longer tasks, they take on more and more information (instructions, tool results, files etc.); eventually this becomes far too much context to comfortably fit in a model's context window . The more history, noise, and tool output a model carries, the worse its accuracy and reasoning tend to get.
In the world of agent engineering, we call this context rot . This blog covers techniques to manage your agent’s context window and how the Deep Agents harness uses a concept called middleware to inject them into your agent’s run.
‍
Understanding context engineering techniques
To simplify, an agent is just a model with a harness around it.
Harness = surrounds the model (LLM) The context engineering techniques at the agent’s disposal to address context rot primarily fall into two categories:
Preventing unnecessary information from entering the context window
Managing and filtering what’s already in the context window
The harness applies these methods strategically to get the model the right context at the right time for the given task.
Now wiring up a harness that does this well is easier said than done, and requires a lot of work (maybe too much work if you are the kind of person who crams for exams the night before).
Deep Agents is LangChain’s open source harness. It wraps the model of your choice with techniques that move context out of the active window (into files, summaries, or a separate agent), so that the main agent carries only what it needs (and can recover the raw data if needed later):
Offloading: large tool results and user messages are saved to the filesystem, and the model sees a preview.
Summarization: when the conversation nears the context limit, older messages are condensed into a summary.
Skills: task know-how loads only when the model decides it's relevant.
Subagents: noisy work runs in a separate context window, and only the result comes back.
Long-term memory: what the agent learns is saved to a file that carries over to the next conversation.
‍
Applying context engineering to common use cases
Let’s see how the techniques above can be applied in a real-world use case: a competitive analysis agent. Every Monday, this agent researches five competitors and writes a report in the team's template. A single run looks something like this:
Pull a market data export for Company A (tens of thousands of rows)
Search the news, read a few articles, and take notes
Repeat for Companies B through E
Draft the report, revise it based on your feedback, and format it
By step 4, the agent has carried five raw exports, dozens of search results, and two stale drafts through every model call. Most of it is irrelevant for formatting the final report.
Retrieval methods ( RAG , or filesystem search) help the agent pull in only what it needs, but that still only solves half the problem. Even a precise agent accumulates unnecessary messages, tool results, and intermediate work, so the harness also has to manage what's already in and around the context window.
‍
How to implement these techniques: middleware
An agent runs in a loop: the model decides what to do, calls a tool, reads the result, and repeats until the task is done. Middleware is code that plugs into specific points in that loop: such as before the agent starts, around each model call, or around each tool call.
At each point it can read the context and change it before the next step runs.
Every context engineering technique in this post is a piece of middleware hooked into one of those points.
Most of this is built in, so you don't need to write any middleware to use these techniques (unless you want to customize something specific).
‍
Offloading: keeping it out the context window
Our agent doesn’t always need to see all the data that’s returned from every tool call or human message, especially if it’s a large volume.
For example, each pull_market_report tool call returns a full data export (thousands of rows); however, the agent only needs a few numbers from it, so the model can be restricted to only see those rows.
Tool Result Offloading process (animated) FilesystemMiddleware runs every time a tool is called:
When a tool result exceeds roughly 20,000 tokens, the full result is written to /large_tool_results/{tool_call_id} before it enters the conversation.
The model sees only a short preview (the first and last few lines) plus the file path.
When the agent later needs Company B's quarterly revenue, it pages through the file with read_file.
Oversized user/human messages, like a pasted call transcript, get the same treatment at a higher threshold (50,000 tokens) and are saved to /conversation_history/.
‍
Summarization: compacting what's already there
Try as we may to offload verbose tool calls, context will gradually begin to pile up over a long run (e.g. five companies' worth of searches, notes, and drafts). Summarization can be used to condense our agent’s entire context window into a summary of what has transpired so far, to allow it to continue on with its research tasks.
Offloading stops the small spikes, while summarization “resets” the overall climb The spikes are large tool results/human messages arriving; offloading swaps each one for a short preview before the model sees it, so context only grows by a little.
Summarization handles the slow climb: once usage hits 85%, older messages are condensed into a summary and context drops back down.
SummarizationMiddleware checks token usage right before each model call:
Once usage crosses a threshold (85% of the model's context window by default), a separate LLM call condenses older messages into a single summary
Older messages are removed from the context window while the most recent messages are kept verbatim.
The model now sees the summary first, then the recent messages (so nothing recent gets paraphrased).

From building your app to growing it: Lovable now helps you find customers
There has probably never been a better time in history to build solutions to big problems. And yet, getting your solution in front of the right audience has never been harder. Reaching customers and growing sales is the most common operational challenge for US small businesses, named by 57% of respondents in a recent study . We hear the same from people building on Lovable. In a survey of more than 400 builders running a business, startup, or side project, a third said they don't know where to start or where to find their customers. Another third had tried nothing beyond posting on social media and asking their network.
The people you are trying to reach have more to look at than ever, and reaching them means showing up where they already look, in search, AI answers, social media, and in the feeds and communities they trust. Lovable now helps you grow your audience across all these channels, from the same chat where you build. In May, every app built with Lovable became readable and indexable by search engines and AI tools . Today, you can go a lot further. Ask Lovable how to grow your app, and it uses the full context of your app to create a growth plan and help you carry it out across organic content and SEO, social media campaigns on Facebook and Instagram or Google Ads campaigns across Search, YouTube, and Maps.
Here's how it works.
Set a goal, get a plan
Tell Lovable what you want, for example "My first 100 signups", "More bookings this month". It reviews what it already knows about your goal, app, target audience, and current traffic, and creates a plan with the actions to take to get there.
Sometimes that's launching an ad campaign. Often, especially for a brand-new app, it's foundational work: making sure your app can be discovered in Google or AI search, sharpening the offer on your landing page, sharing your app across social media, finding leads and talking to potential customers, or making sure your local business shows up on Google Maps. Lovable will suggest the next steps based on your own context, and you review and approve before acting on any recommendations.
You can change the goal at any time, and Lovable iterates with you.
Launch ads on Google, YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram directly from Lovable
To start reaching and converting high-intent customers on Google Search, Maps, and YouTube, simply ask Lovable to connect your existing Google Ads account or create one. Lovable will install a Google Tag to measure the conversions that matter to your goal, and recommend the right campaign type.
Once your campaign is live, Google's built-in AI connects you with your ideal audience at the right time, whether they're searching on Google or watching their favorite videos on YouTube. If you're new to Google Ads you could qualify for Google Ads credits to jumpstart your first campaign.
To reach new users across Facebook and Instagram, sign in with Facebook Login for Business and Lovable connects to your ad account and Facebook Page. If you don't have them yet, you can create both in the same sign-in window. Lovable then adds the Meta Pixel to your app. The Pixel is a small piece of code that records when a visitor does the thing you care about, like signing up or buying, so you can see what your ads produce. If you don't have a Pixel, Lovable creates one for you. From there, Lovable builds image and video campaigns for Facebook and Instagram with a Sales, Leads, or Traffic objective.
After creating your campaign, review by Meta starts right away. Once your campaign is approved, you can launch it when you're ready.
You approve before anything spends
Before a campaign is created, Lovable summarizes the key inputs for your review: daily budget, target locations, languages, goals, and tracking. No ad campaigns will go live until you approve them.
Billing for your campaigns is set up directly within your Google Ads and Meta account. Lovable does not bill you directly or add a service fee to your ad spend. Creating and iterating on the growth plan and generating ad assets consumes regular Lovable credits.
Once a campaign is running, results show up in the Analytics tab, or you can ask Lovable for help analyzing performance in the chat. Ask it to pause, change the budget, reach a different audience, or try new copy, and Lovable applies the change. Ask for a dashboard, and it builds one. Lovable suggests what to change and makes the changes you ask for, but will not change a campaign on its own.
Be found in search with better SEO
Ranking in search takes three things working together: the fundamentals that let search engines and AI tools read your app, content people want to read, and links from places they already trust. Lovable now helps with all three.
It starts with the fundamentals: indexable pages, metadata and titles, sitemap, robots.txt, and connecting to Google Search Console. Lovable checks them in the SEO review and can fix what's off.
With Semrush built in, Lovable then finds what your app can realistically rank for, reviews how your existing pages perform, and is able to create the landing pages and content to rank for people, AI search, and agents.
The third part is new. Based on what you've built and who it's for, Lovable recommends where your product should show up beyond your own site: the forums, communities, directories, and social platforms where your audience already spends time, and where a mention can earn you a backlink as well as a visitor. Lovable drafts the posts and profiles for you. You publish them from your own accounts, so the voice and the relationships stay yours.
Creative assets made from your app
Lovable can create images, launch videos, animated product demos, video ads, landing pages, ad copy, and social media posts based on your product and brand identity. Before proposing anything, Lovable researches search interest for your topic and what similar businesses are running, and writes a short research report you can read. Then it proposes three creative directions. Pick one, adjust it, or upload your own images and videos instead.
Get started
Available today on Free, Pro, and Business plans. On Enterprise, an admin enables app and chat connectors under Connectors → Admin settings.
Open a published project and ask Lovable how to win more customers. Read the docs if you want the details first.
Building is just the beginning. The harder part comes after: finding the people your app is for and turning them into signups, customers, or bookings. Now Lovable helps you with that too. Try it out in Lovable now or read more .

items.title: Gemini 4 Argon 全面开放，作者实测后认为难以撼动 Claude Opus 5.5 和 GPT-6 Astra
items.title_en: 实测Gemini 4 Argon - Google这跌跌撞撞的背水一战。
items.summary: Google 于10月14日全面开放 Gemini 4 Argon，作者实测后认为其很难冲击 Claude Opus 5.5 和 GPT-6 Astra 的地位。
items.fullContent:
X 上的 数字生命卡兹克：“https://t.co/NQPgzXsTUS” / X
文章
登录 注册
文章
登录 注册
数字生命卡兹克
@Khazix0918
实测Gemini 4 Argon - Google这跌跌撞撞的背水一战。
67
13
294
117
就在今晚，Gemini 4 Argon，终于全面开放了。
其实这玩意，10月1号就已经官宣过一次了，就在OpenAI开完DevDay的第二天。
但是那一次，基本上就是纯官宣，没啥人能用上，只给一个叫Fairwind的网络安全计划开放，基本都是政府、关键基础设施、安全公司啊这些做防守的人。
终于在憋了两周之后，Google选在今天官宣了。
这一个多月，基本上新的大模型就是轮番轰炸，我简单顺了一下节奏。
9月4号，GPT-6 Astra。
9月22号，Grok 4.7。
9月23号，Claude Opus 5.5、GPT-6 Sol和Luna，一夜三连发。
9月30号，OpenAI DevDay，GPT-6.1 Sol。
10月1号，Gemini 4 Argon官宣。
10月13号，Meta的第一个前沿模型，Muse Wonder。
10月14号，Gemini 4 Argon全面开放。
基本上海外的几个巨头都到齐了，不过在模型层面，目前Anthropic还是无可争议的T0梯队，然后是OpenAI紧随其后，Meta和Google奋力追赶，Grok还在玩泥巴中。
我已经很久没有给Gemini付过费了，今晚又给他们贡献了100美刀，升级了一下Ultra会员，来体验一下Gemini 4 Argon。
最终几个小时体验下来，我个人觉得，还是很难冲击Claude Opus 5.5和GPT-6 Astra的地位。
一个一个说吧。
一. Google这大半年
在聊Argon之前，我觉得得先聊聊谷歌这大半年。
大家才能更加对这个模型的使命有一些理解。。。
时间拨回去年11月，Gemini 3 Pro发布，那个时候，它可以说是全世界最好的模型之一。
然后，谷歌就开始了一段非常魔幻的日子。
2月份发了个Gemini 3.1 Pro，然后在5月的I/O上，承诺一个月内发Gemini 3.5 Pro。
结果一拖再拖，说3.5 Pro的进度落后了好几个月，其中一个原因，是代码能力没达到内部目标，没办法，Anthropic和OpenAI给的压力太大了。
结果最后拖着拖着，内部直接砍掉了。。。
然后8月5号，谷歌AI这边，直接大换血。
哈萨比斯卸任Google DeepMind的CEO，改当DeepMind董事长兼Alphabet首席科学家，然后由科雷接手。
同一天，在谷歌干了27年的传奇Jeff，也就是大家口中的“姐夫”，宣布离职，出去创业。
姐夫是1999年加入谷歌的，那时候谷歌还是个小公司。
后来撑起整个谷歌的那些底层技术，MapReduce、BigTable、Spanner，都有他的名字，基本是他跟老搭档桑杰，两个人坐在一台电脑前结对写出来的。
2011年，他和吴恩达等人一起创立了Google Brain，后来又带队做出了TensorFlow。
再后来Google Brain和DeepMind合并，他当上了Google DeepMind的首席科学家，也是Gemini的技术负责人之一。
谷歌后来专门为他和桑杰两个人，设了一个新的最高职级，11级。
程序员圈子里甚至有个流传了快20年的梗，叫Jeff Dean Facts，专门编段子吹他。
比如：“编译器从来不给Jeff报警告，是Jeff给编译器报警告。”、“光在真空里的速度原来只有每小时35英里，后来Jeff Dean花了一个周末，优化了一下物理学。”之类的。。。
就是这么一个神一样的人，走了。
跟他一起走的，还有桑杰。
两天后，SemiAnalysis直接发了一篇文章，标题叫：
Gemini is Cooked but GCP is Cooking。
翻译过来就是，Gemini凉透了，但谷歌云正在起飞。
因为谷歌把大把的TPU算力，卖给了Anthropic这些对手，自家模型拉完了，但是卖铲子的生意反而越做越大。
这大半年里，谷歌基本就是靠Flash系列在续命，从3.5 Flash一路发到9月2号的3.8 Flash，这大概就是OpenAI再也掏不出来Astra了，天天发Luna，Anthropic也做不出来Fable了，天天发Haiku。
你就说魔幻不魔幻吧。。。
所以Argon对谷歌来说，真的不是一次普通的模型发布。
这是谷歌的，背水一战。
二. 基本信息
惯例先总结一下基本信息。
目前Gemini 4 Argon已经上线，20刀的Pro会员可以在Gemini APP里面用。
但是呢，如果你想在Antigravity（也就是Google家的Claude Code、Codex）里面去用，你必须要开100刀的Ultra会员才能用。
这一点非常的蛋疼。。。
然后，果不其然的就被喷了。
推理强度有三档，低中高，虽然他们这个翻译让我觉得团队里没有任何一个懂中文的人了。
模型上，Gemini一贯的传统，是个多模态的模型，支持视频、声音、图片、文字等几乎全模态的输入。
知识截止日期是2026年3月，比GPT-6 Astra和Claude Opus 5.5都要旧一点。
上下文这块，有个小细节。
9月30号官宣的时候，谷歌的说法是，输出上限从上一代的6.4万Token，直接拉到100万。
但是今天的说法，变成了“输入输出合计100万”，也就是你的输入、思考、输出共享了，还配了一个所谓的续写协议，continuation protocol。
这玩意的意思就是，Argon一次请求，最多还是只能吐6.4万Token左右，跟上一代差不多，写到上限了，它不会直接断掉，会返回一个加密的续写令牌，里面记着它前面写到了哪，然后开发者再拿着这个令牌，把原来的请求原封不动再发一遍，它就接着往下写。
就这么一段一段接下去，最多能接到100万。。。
GPT-6 Astra原生单次最高输出甚至是128K，比Gemini 4 Argon还高点。。。
然后是价格。
现在是优惠期，2美刀/输入、10美刀/输出，跟GPT-6.1 Sol、Claude Sonnet 5.5，是同一个价。
但是优惠期是11月30号到期，优惠期一过，就变成4美刀/输入、20美刀/输出，就跟Claude Opus 5.5一模一样了。
但是对Agent来说，真正的大头，其实是缓存，对比一下。
Gemini 4 Argon，优惠期0.1美元，12月1号以后0.2美元。
GPT-6.1 Sol，0.1美元。
Claude Sonnet 5.5，0.1美元，这个是10月7号刚从0.2美元降下来的。
Claude Opus 5.5，0.2美元。
GPT-6 Astra，1美元。

Just five months ago, when we announced our Series C, I wrote that demand was accelerating . Since then, usage has tripled and we’ve grown more than 15x year-over-year. We recently crossed $1B in annualized run rate with no sign of slowing down.
Software can do things that were impossible just a few years ago
It’s clear that AI has unlocked a whole new set of software capabilities. So many incredible applications exist now that couldn’t have been built before. The old stack doesn’t quite fit them. They need different building blocks and a new way to think about infrastructure.
We’re powering a ton of these applications. Among them is TypeSafe AI’s Jev, one of the fastest-growing products ever. It served 1T tokens on Modal in its first three days, and the TypeSafe team stayed focused on shipping instead of managing infrastructure.
And it’s happening in many different verticals
DoorDash’s AI platform team uses Modal to get apps across the company from experiment to production. Cognition, Ramp, Linear, and Hebbia are building background agents that are experts in their fields. Runway is generating life-like video, in every region of the world. Physical Intelligence, Generalist AI, and 1X are training robots. Chai Discovery and Achira run drug discovery on Modal, as do scientists working through Claude Science .
Every shift needs new infrastructure
Every shift in software changes both what people can build and the infrastructure they need to build it. I've been writing software since the early nineties, and this isn't the first step-change: we've had the web, the cloud, big data, mobile, and several other shifts.
When the cloud started, suddenly you had to deal with distributed systems, sharding, and config management. None of our original tools were built for it, so developers created new ones: Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, etc.
The friction with AI is pretty clear by now. GPUs are scarce, and models are quite large and slow to load. LLMs write code now! And it has to run somewhere, isolated from everything else. Sure, you can build for all of those considerations on the old stack, and plenty of people have, but you end up in YAML hell and GPU procurement purgatory.
So we went deep. We threw out most of the existing stack and built our own file system, container runtime, scheduler, and networking from the ground up, on a capacity pool that now spans 20+ clouds.
What developers need is better building blocks
The beauty of software is composability. If you have the right building blocks — general-purpose, battle-tested, and scalable — there’s infinite combinations of things you can build.
Functions were our first building block: you write code, and Modal runs it. This turned out to be incredibly useful, especially for Gen AI: image generation with diffusion models, music at Suno, LLM inference with SGLang and vLLM, and model training.
We launched Sandboxes in 2023 when we noticed that people were using LLMs to generate code. Sandboxes exploded and three years later, it’s a $300M run rate product just on its own. Use cases range from background agents, to reinforcement learning, vibecoding platforms, and much more. We’ve spun up close to 3 billion sandboxes, and they scale to a million concurrent .
We’re launching a lot more
A new world of software capabilities requires a new set of building blocks and we’re just getting started.
We recently launched multi-node training – one decorator gives you a fully RDMA-connected cluster with no capacity commitment. We’re moving up the stack and launching a number of products in RL and post-training as well.
On the inference side, we’ve been launching Modal servers , which is a better solution for HTTP servers, as well as some really cool features around LLM serving, such as Endpoint Candidates .
With Sandboxes, virtual machines are now generally available.
These are just a few of the many more developments to come.
We’ve raised more capital
When we started Modal five years ago, I couldn't have imagined most of the applications running on it today. It's just as difficult to imagine the software people will be creating two years from now, but what I do know is that it's going to require an entirely new set of building blocks. We want a lot of it to run on Modal.
To keep building what's next, we’ve raised a $750M Series D at a $15.75B post-money valuation. Accel led the round. Kleiner Perkins joined, and all of our existing investors participated, including Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital, Amplify Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures.
I'm obviously biased, but I can't think of a better time to be building software.

Today, we’re announcing Grok Voice 3.0, the world’s most intelligent speech-to-speech model. items.title_en: Adaptive Verification Without a Confidence Head
items.summary: vLLM 支持 confidence scoring 扩展到所有基于草稿模型的投机类型，通过在线拟合的 logistic 回归从草发者 logits 推导 logit(q_max) 特征来预测目标模型的接受概率，作为 Adaptive Verification 的置信分。
items.fullContent:
Adaptive Verification Without a Confidence Head | vLLM Blog
Menu
Theme
Table of Contents
Adaptive Verification with an online-fitted acceptance estimator TL;DR
Confidence scoring is now supported for all draft-model-based speculator types. In the absence of a confidence head, an online-fitted estimator derives a feature from the drafter's logits to predict the target model's probability of accepting it, which is used directly as a confidence score for Adaptive Verification. The estimator's coefficients are continuously fitted, adapting to the incoming data traffic. This feature landed in PR #52228 , and is enabled with enable_adaptive_verification for draft models without a confidence head.
Background
vLLM's Adaptive Verification (AV) enables verification of a subset of the drafted tokens during speculative decoding. Draft tokens with low probability of acceptance are trimmed from the batch before running the target model's forward pass, saving on compute. This optimization is particularly beneficial while serving large batch sizes, because in that regime the GPU becomes compute-bound. See this vLLM blog post for more details.
AV needs a per-token estimate of acceptance probability, which is why, until now, it only supported DSpark drafters. DSpark models often ship with a confidence head: a small linear layer over the drafter's hidden state for each position, trained as a binary classifier for "will the target accept this token?"
Problem
Draft models that lack a confidence head, such as EAGLE, MTP, DFlash, and some DSpark checkpoints, miss out on AV entirely. To use it, these drafters need a per-token acceptance estimate, and adding a confidence head means retraining the drafter, which isn't an option for the many existing checkpoints that people already serve.
Prior Work
Using the drafter's own confidence as a proxy for acceptance is well established. EAGLE-2 showed that EAGLE's draft probabilities closely track acceptance rates, and used them to grow and rerank a dynamic draft tree. Draft & Verify and several follow-ups stop drafting once the drafter's probability falls below a fixed threshold. SpecDec++ instead trains a dedicated acceptance-prediction head, similar in spirit to DSpark's confidence head. In each case, the mapping from draft confidence to acceptance is either used as-is or learned offline.
AV needs more than a good ranking. Its budget decision sums predicted acceptance probabilities and weighs them against measured costs, so the predictions must be calibrated for the specific model pair and workload being served, which is what the online-fitted estimator in the next section provides.
Solution: Online-Fitted Acceptance Estimator
We added a lightweight logistic regression that estimates each draft token's acceptance probability from a single scalar derived from the draft distribution, the log-odds of the drafter's most likely token. It has one shared slope and one intercept per draft position, so a K -token drafter needs a total of K + 1 parameters. Those parameters are fitted online from the accept/reject decisions the target model already produces during normal verification. Any existing draft checkpoint gets AV for free.
The rest of this section covers the two halves of the design: what quantity the estimator scores, and how its coefficients are fitted during serving.
Scoring the Distribution
The confidence score for a given draft token is estimated using a per-position logistic regression:
where ω is the fitted slope shared across all draft positions, β i is the fitted per-position intercept, and q is the draft distribution. The alternate log-odds form makes the relationship clear:
logit( q max ) is the estimator's feature, and is the log-odds of the draft's most likely token. Intuitively, it represents how confident the draft model is in its predictions. It is transformed linearly by the coefficients ω and β i to predict the log-odds of the draft's acceptance by the target model. The sigmoid of that is p , the estimated acceptance rate, which is used as the confidence score for AV.
Other Considered Features
Several alternative features were considered and rejected for one reason or another. The four main axes that we cared most about when evaluating a feature were:
Losslessness — Whether the feature biases the output distribution during speculative decoding.
Area Under the Curve (AUC) — The probability that a randomly chosen accepted draft scores higher than a randomly selected rejected one. This measures discrimination between drafts that should be accepted vs rejected. A higher value indicates a better ability to discriminate, and 0.5 is random chance.
Log-loss — The mean negative log-likelihood of the predicted acceptance probability, which penalizes confident wrong answers and rewards calibration. A lower value indicates a better ability to predict the true acceptance probability of a given draft.
Expected Calibration Error (ECE) — Bin each draft based on its predicted acceptance probability, then measure the error between the mean prediction vs the mean observed frequency within each bin, weighted by the bin occupancy. This measures calibration , and a lower value indicates a better ability to assign a probability to a draft that matches the true frequency among drafts scored similarly.
Losslessness is a non-negotiable property for the features to have. Otherwise, we break the fundamental guarantee of speculative decoding to output the target model's exact distribution. AUC and ECE both matter for AV's trimming decision, but in different ways. AUC is important for the local ordering of survival probabilities:
survival = confidence_probs[idx_mapping].cumprod( dim = 1 ) ... winners = flat.topk(draft_budget).indices
AUC ensures that a more likely to be accepted draft token is admitted over a less likely one. On the other hand, ECE is important for the global budget decision:
num_tokens_to_estimated_accepted_tokens = np.concatenate( ([num_sampling_requests], num_sampling_requests + np.cumsum(scores)) ) costs = draft_cost_ms[ ... ] + verify_cost_ms[ ... ] ... draft_budget = int (np.argmax(num_tokens_to_estimated_accepted_tokens / costs))
The probabilities are summed and then divided by the measured cost table. ECE ensures that the estimated number of accepted tokens matches reality.
Below is a table of the various experimented features, along with their scores for the four categories. They were measured over ~4.5M labeled drafts collected over the course of serving DeepSeek-V4-Flash + DSpark (temp=1, top-p=0.95, conc=64), without AV, across five datasets: SPEED-Bench 2k low/high-entropy, GSM8K, HumanEval, and MT-Bench. The last two rows are references rather than fitted features: the drafter's q max used directly as the acceptance probability with no fit, and the trained confidence head's scores.
feature lossless AUC log-loss ECE log( q max ) yes 0.8069 0.4813 0.0592 log( q max ) − log( q 2nd ) (top-2 margin) yes 0.8156 0.4437 0.0105 H ( q ) (entropy) yes 0.8321 0.4577 0.0638 −log(−log( q max )) yes 0.8336 0.4289 0.0103 logit( q max ) (shipped) yes 0.8336 0.4284 0.0100 logit( q sampled ) no 0.8553 0.4040 0.0152 −log(−log( q sampled )) no 0.8554 0.4075 0.0193 q max (no fit, used directly as the probability) yes 0.8259 0.4880 0.0736 trained confidence head yes 0.8191 0.4449 0.0052
logit( q sampled ) and −log(−log( q sampled )) clearly outperform the chosen feature in the table in terms of AUC, but were not used because trimming based on them results in a biased output distribution. Both read q sampled , the probability of the token the drafter actually drew. Trimming a draft on a function of this value makes the decision to verify at position i dependent on x i itself, so the drafts that survive trimming are no longer distributed as q . Standard rejection sampling accepts a token with probability min(1, p / q ), expecting q to be the distribution the draft token was sampled from. But trimming based on q sampled biases the emitted distribution towards the drafter's higher confidence tokens. 1
The q max "no fit" row shows why we fit at all, instead of using the drafter's own probability directly, as EAGLE-2 does when building its draft tree. Used directly, the drafter's top-token probability actually ranks drafts better than the trained confidence head (0.8259 vs 0.8191 AUC). However, it is not well calibrated. Its mean prediction over the labeled drafts is 0.784 against the observed acceptance rate of 0.723, and its ECE is 7x worse than the shipped logit( q max ) feature (0.0736 vs 0.0100). The drafter's top-token probability reflects only how confident the drafter is in its own prediction, not whether the target model will agree. This agreement is further influenced by the sampling setup and the workload. An online fit learns this mapping directly from the target's accept/reject decisions, yielding better calibration, which is what the budget decision depends on.
We ultimately went with the logit( q max ) feature, which has a good balance of AUC and ECE at a reasonable cost. It was also a natural choice, since it shares both the log-odds scale and the resolution of the quantity we were trying to estimate.
Versus a Trained Confidence Head
As seen in the table above, for DeepSeek-V4-Flash + DSpark, the estimator outperforms the confidence head in both AUC and log-likelihood loss, but underperforms in ECE. The table below summarizes the difference:
AUC ↑ log-loss ↓ ECE ↓ estimator logit( q max ) 0.8336 0.4284 0.0100 trained confidence head 0.8191 0.4449 0.0052 Δ (estimator − head) +0.0146 −0.0166 +0.0048
However, once we exclude the first draft from the averages, the picture changes substantially:
AUC ↑ log-loss ↓ ECE ↓ estimator logit( q max ) 0.8352 0.4420 0.0103 trained confidence head 0.8075 0.4743 0.0090 Δ (estimator − head) +0.0278 −0.0323 +0.0013
The head and estimator are now virtually tied on calibration. The per-position AUC breakdown helps explain why:
Per-position AUC for the online estimator and the trained confidence head on DeepSeek-V4-Flash + DSpark at 7 speculative tokens, over 4.47M labeled drafts. The head leads at the first position; the estimator leads from the second onwards, and both fall off past the fifth position. The confidence head is the better predictor on the first draft position, but the estimator takes the lead from the second position onwards. The gap widens with depth, with the estimator leading by 0.08 AUC by the last position. Both predictors also fall off after the fifth position. This is likely because DSV4-Flash's DSpark declares a block size of 5 and the drafter was never trained past it, so the drafts themselves get worse there.
Since survival is a running product, and the first draft position always carries a request's highest score, it is less often the token that the budget cuts. The estimator's advantage sits right where the trimming happens, and it explains why the estimator can match the confidence head in end-to-end performance.
Fitting the Coefficients
The coefficients ω and β i are continuously refitted during live serving of requests. Draft tokens proposed during the previous decode step are verified by the target model in the next decode step. Only draft tokens up until the first rejection (if any) are eligible for training on, because the target model has explicitly labeled them (accept or reject).
We use Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS) to minimize the log-likelihood loss of the predictions vs the labels. This minimization is performed over a second-order Taylor approximation of the log-likelihood loss. The optimization step for ω and β i is obtained by solving the system of equations
where Δ θ is the delta for the shared slope ω and the per-position intercepts β i , H is the Hessian of the loss function with a shape of ( K + 1) × ( K + 1), and g is the gradient of the loss function, with a size of K + 1.
A refit happens after every fixed round of N decode steps. During each decode step in that interval, we accumulate the Hessian and gradient values, which are derived from the coefficients, features, and labels collected during the round. Doing this upper bounds memory to O ( K ²) across a round, in contrast with O ( N × B × K ) if we instead collected the raw labels. On the final step of the round, the system is solved, and the coefficients are updated.
As one might expect, deeper drafts are accepted less often than shallower drafts. Consequently, deeper draft positions can be starved of labels during a round. Two design decisions were made to mitigate the impact of this on the refitting process:
Shared Slope : The slope is shared across all draft positions to prevent noisy updates caused by data thinning at depth. Predictions are much more sensitive to slope errors than intercept errors, so sharing makes the Newton step well-determined. Furthermore, empirical measurements show sharing the slope costs virtually nothing in terms of accuracy (only 0.0002 AUC and 0.0003 log-loss).
Step Damping : Each coefficient's update is scaled by the amount of supporting evidence using the formula n / ( n + constant), where n is the count of graded drafts. This ensures that deeper positions with fewer labels move more conservatively, preventing updates based on noise.
Slope vs Intercept Roles
The fitted coefficients were tracked across several model/dataset combinations, and the two kinds of parameters behave very differently.
Hold the model pair fixed and vary the workload : Fitting DSV4-Flash + DSpark independently on each of five workloads, the slope barely moves (0.51 to 0.55), uncorrelated with how hard the workload is (r = −0.08 against mean draft entropy). The intercepts do the opposite: the first draft position intercept correlates with draft entropy at r = −0.89, and runs from ~0.5–0.6 on the more predictable workloads down to below 0 on the least.
Dataset Acceptance Rate Mean Draft Entropy Slope ω Intercept β 0 gsm8k 0.781 0.562 0.5365 +0.478 humaneval 0.751 0.669 0.5135 +0.486 speed-bench 2k low-entropy 0.755 0.703 0.5087 +0.610 mt-bench 0.714 0.800 0.5495 +0.181 speed-bench 2k high-entropy 0.642 1.077 0.5197 −0.089
Now vary the model pair: The slope ranges from 0.45 to 0.59 across pairs, while staying tight within each one. The intercepts also differ between pairs, so unlike the slope they are not a property of one axis alone.
Model nspec Slope ω ω sd Intercept β 0 DeepSeek-V4-Flash + DSpark 5 0.5013 0.0250 +0.279 MiMo-V2.5-Pro-FP4 + DFlash 8 0.5197 0.0415 −1.000 Inkling-NVFP4 + MTP 8 0.5859 0.0349 −0.572 Muse-Glimmer-30B + DFlash2 7 0.4450 0.0323 +0.167
Read together, the two tables suggest a division of labor. The slope measures how well the draft model knows when it's right. This is a property of the target/draft pair and the draft sampling method, which is why it barely moves when only the workload changes. The intercepts absorb the rest: the base acceptance rate at each draft position, which falls with depth and drops even further on less predictable content. That base acceptance rate depends on the model pair as well as the workload, which is why the intercepts move along both axes while the slope moves along just one.
Benchmarks
We benchmarked three checkpoints (MiMo-V2.5-Pro-FP4 + DFlash, Inkling-NVFP4 + MTP, and Muse-Glimmer-30B + DFlash2) that previously could not use AV at all, along with DSV4-Flash + DSpark + the estimator, and DSV4-Flash + DSpark + the confidence head, as a reference. The gains below were captured with AV off vs on, temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, and concurrency 64, over four datasets.
Output throughput gain from Adaptive Verification, AV off vs on, for MiMo-V2.5-Pro, Inkling-NVFP4, Muse-Glimmer-30B, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash + DSpark with both the online estimator and the confidence head, across four datasets at concurrency 64 Compared to fixed verification, the online estimator at the same speculative length is a win across all benchmarked datasets. However, that gain alone doesn't tell the whole story. Oftentimes, a smaller fixed length can be found to outperform AV at the max speculative length at specific concurrencies. The Pareto curve below was captured with DSV4 + DSpark across a sweep of fixed speculative lengths and AV at the max speculative length:
Throughput versus interactivity for DeepSeek-V4-Flash + DSpark across fixed speculative lengths and Adaptive Verification with the online estimator and the confidence head The online estimator and the confidence head are roughly on par in terms of performance, across all measured concurrencies. However, the online estimator is not meant to be a replacement for the confidence head, but rather a drop-in alternative in the absence of one. Let's see how it performs on a model pair that currently lacks a confidence head. Below is the Pareto curve for MiMo-V2.5-Pro-FP4 + DFlash across a sweep of fixed speculative lengths and AV:
Throughput versus interactivity for MiMo-V2.5-Pro-FP4 + DFlash across fixed speculative lengths and Adaptive Verification with the online estimator AV sits on the throughput-interactivity frontier at 5 of 7 concurrencies.
Limitations
The target model's attention backend must support variable-length verification. This is the same prerequisite that DSpark AV already has.
MTP and EAGLE benefit less from AV than DFlash and DSpark do. This is because those auto-regressive speculators pay a proportionally larger cost for drafting tokens that may get trimmed before verification.
vLLM Usage
AV is enabled through the speculative config. On a draft model that (1) has no confidence head and (2) supports variable length attention for all of its backends, the online estimator is selected automatically:
vllm serve < target_mode l > \ ... --speculative-config '{ "model": "<draft_model>", "method": "<method>", "num_speculative_tokens": <num_speculative_tokens>, "draft_sample_method": "probabilistic", "enable_adaptive_verification": true }'
Acknowledgements
This work was done by Giancarlo Delfin (Inferact), and builds directly on Adaptive Verification by Lucas Wilkinson (Red Hat) and Benjamin Chislett (NVIDIA).
Footnotes
An example with a simple two-token vocabulary of [ a , b ] can be used to illustrate this bias. Assume p = [0.5, 0.5], q = [0.2, 0.8], and that a draft token is trimmed from verification if q ( x ) < 0.5. Drawing a results in trimming, and the target samples a token from its own distribution, p ( x ). However, drawing b results in verification: the token is accepted with probability min(1, p ( b )/ q ( b )) = 0.625, and otherwise rejected and resampled from the residual norm(max(0, p − q )) = [1, 0], yielding a . During rejection sampling we get p out ( a ) = q ( a )· p ( a ) + q ( b )·(1 − 0.625) = 0.4 and p out ( b ) = q ( a )· p ( b ) + q ( b )·0.625 = 0.6. This differs from the target's distribution of [0.5, 0.5] and violates speculative decoding's lossless guarantee. ↩

items.title: Google 发布智能体审稿系统 Deep Review，支持多领域技术文档审查
items.title_en: Analyzing technical documents with Deep Review
items.summary: Google 公开发布智能体审阅系统 Deep Review，可对复杂技术文档提供反馈与验证，最初面向计算机科学论文，现已扩展到法律、金融等领域。
items.fullContent:
Analyzing technical documents with Deep Review Skip to main content
Google Research
Search
Analyzing technical documents with Deep Review
October 14, 2026
Rajesh Jayaram and Vincent Cohen-Addad, Research Scientists, Google Research
Following successful deployments across 16,000+ submissions at STOC, ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR, Deep Review is launching publicly. It’s expanding from deep mathematical and scientific peer review to provide rigorous, grounded verification across knowledge documents, including Google Docs and presentations.
Quick links
Paper
STOC 2026 Blog Post
ICML 2026 Retrospective
NeurIPS 2026 Blog Post
Google Labs Portal
R@ Top 10 Blog
News from Google R@ Collection Page
Share
Copy link
×
Generative AI has accelerated many technical fields. It is now common for AI to play some role in writing scientific papers and technical documents, running code, designing experiments, and drafting proposals. However, accelerating content creation has created a review challenge: the human capacity for verification has remained largely fixed amid this rapid increase in AI-generated content. Reviewing complex documents like long scientific manuscripts or complex legal agreements requires specialized expertise and advanced subject knowledge. This imbalance creates a validation bottleneck , where information is being generated faster than it can be rigorously reviewed.
Today, we’re excited to announce the public release of Deep Review , an agentic AI system engineered to provide rigorous feedback and technical verification on complex documents. Initially designed for computer science academic paper analysis, the system’s capabilities have expanded to review documents across many domains, such as legal and finance. It can be used as both an iterative improvement tool during the drafting process and a tool for the scientific process verification, claims, and evaluation during the review process.
Deep Review represents the evolution of our Paper Assistant Tool (PAT) — an experimental initiative developed to help researchers stress-test manuscripts prior to conference submission. Over the past year, we partnered with four flagship computer science conferences ( STOC 2026 , ICML 2026, NeurIPS 2026, and ICLR 2027 ) to provide private, pre-submission feedback to authors of more than 16,000 manuscripts who opted in. Further details on PAT and these pilots can be found in our manuscript, Towards Automating Scientific Review with Google’s Paper Assistant Tool .
With this release, Deep Review is now accessible worldwide:
Tiered access and scalable API : Every user receives two complimentary document reviews per week. Users with high-volume workflows can connect their Gemini API key for higher usage limits and programmatic integration via the Deep Review API.
Format flexibility : Deep Review will initially support PDFs and plain text as input formats, with support for multi-file inputs coming soon.
Privacy and data policy : Documents uploaded to Deep Review are never used to train, fine-tune, or improve Google models. Uploaded documents are stored for one year for the sole purpose of display to the user in the Deep Review UI.
Deep Review accelerates technical validation
One of the most significant examples of the validation bottleneck is in academic peer review. This can be seen in the uptick of submissions to academic publication venues, especially venues for AI research itself, which have seen a dramatic rise. This year, there were over 74,000 submissions to three major AI conferences ( ICLR , NeurIPS , and ICML ) up from approximately 45,000 in 2025, 32,000 in 2024, and 23,000 in 2023. Each of these submissions requires multiple high-quality reviews to ensure the integrity of the peer review process, which can place a larger burden on human experts.
Increase in submissions to NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR between 2023 and 2026.
Deep Review aims to help alleviate this expanding burden on human reviewers across technical fields. By providing detailed, objective evaluations of documents, Deep Review checks logical consistency and mathematical statements, suggests improvements, grounds facts, and compares with existing work. It addresses some of the most cognitively burdensome facets of review, while leaving higher-level judgements to humans.
A proven track record for scientific review
Deep Review has been extensively tested and deployed under its experimental name, the Paper Assistant Tool (PAT), in four pilot partnerships with the flagship computer science conferences STOC 2026, ICML 2026, NeurIPS 2026, and ICLR 2027. During these pilots, authors were able to opt-in to receive feedback and analysis on their paper via PAT in the weeks before the submission deadline. The goal was to provide authors with actionable feedback to help improve the quality of papers in submission. This feedback was completely decoupled from the official conference review process. PAT did not collect any of the data for training, and papers were deleted from Google systems promptly after each program concluded.
Author reactions to the tool have been extremely positive, and reflect continued improvements to both underlying models and the PAT harness. With the addition of Gemini 4 Argon support in Deep Review, the underlying capabilities of the tool have further increased beyond the older iterations of PAT described below.
Statistics and author feedback from the pilot programs of PAT at machine learning and theoretical computer science conferences.
How Deep Review works
Single-prompt LLM calls often fail when evaluating long, complex documents due to exhausting their token reasoning budget, overlooking long-context cross-section dependencies, or accepting nuanced claims without fully scrutinizing them. Deep Review solves these challenges through a four-stage agentic pipeline:
Document segmentation : The document is first ingested and autonomously decomposed by a segmenter agent into logical segments (e.g., Introduction, experiments, methodology, etc.). These segments can be overlapping, and must cover all the content of the input document.
Adaptive budgeting : Not all sections require equal cognitive depth. The pipeline inspects information density and dynamically allocates a compute budget, along with a specialized inference scaling pipeline for each section. For instance, sections with dense mathematical proofs may receive more compute than an introduction or a related work section in an academic paper.
Deep parallel verification : Specialized reasoning agents scrutinize each segment in parallel. Each agent has access to the full document context to track cross-references, but focuses its reasoning power specifically on the task of reviewing its specific target section. This ensures both that reviewing tasks are manageable for each review swarm, and that parallel swarms are properly coordinated.
Global synthesis and agentic grounding : A dedicated synthesis agent consolidates the segment-level reports, and does final consistency checks between sections, rerunning logical checks if required. The agent further performs external grounding checks and tool calls as a final preventative measure against hallucinations.
System architecture showing the four-stage pipeline.
Universal verification and review: Beyond research papers
While Deep Review originated in academic paper reviews, long-context review is generalizable: reasoning mechanisms used to check whether a mathematical proof holds up in a research paper can also help surface logical gaps and inconsistencies in other types of documents, where claims must be backed by evidence. Therefore, Deep Review can be used to bring structured critique to a broader range of everyday workflows.
Users can now apply Deep Review to analyze complex documents across many domains. For instance, it can be run on:
Design documents: Catch unstated architectural assumptions, spot edge cases, and suggest concrete improvements.
Presentations: Ensure slide transitions flow logically and bulleted takeaways match visual charts.
Legal and financial documents: Check internal consistency across clauses and data tables, flag ambiguous terms or downstream consequences, and ground claims against supporting evidence.
Deep Review meets Antigravity
We’re also introducing the Teamwork Deep Document Review Pattern , a document review implementation pattern inspired by Deep Review built into Antigravity using the Teamwork multi-agent orchestration framework . This pattern is designed systematically to evaluate research papers, manuscript drafts, and technical proposals using a multi-agent hierarchy with self-correction and segment-based rubrics. Antigravity users can invoke this pattern using the /teamwork-preview command.
Making thorough, high-quality technical reviews widely accessible
Comprehensive pre-submission critique in computer science has generally depended on access to extensive review networks — like senior faculty, well-resourced academic laboratories, or extensive peer advisory networks. Providing reliable, automated logical verification can help many academics stress-test their assertions, identify avoidable flaws, refine and strengthen their documents based on verified foundations, and present their work in a review process with more confidence.
Get started
We invite researchers, engineers, and creators everywhere to explore Deep Review:
Try Deep Review: Visit the Google Research Portal to review your first documents.
Integrate with the API: Access programmatic verification in your continuous integration and drafting workflows using your Gemini API key .
Read the research: Read the preprint to explore the underlying methodology and pilot evaluations.
Conclusion and looking ahead
Given the utility it demonstrated during our pilot programs with academic conferences, we believe that tools like Deep Review will play a significant role across the peer review process in the coming years by empowering both authors and reviewers.
Moving forward, we are continuing to expand the platform’s capabilities. With the rollout of Gemini 4 Argon support, Deep Review’s underlying capabilities further improve, delivering even higher quality feedback and analysis to authors. Additionally, with multi-file support coming soon, users will also be able to run these same consistency checks across entire sets of related documents, spreadsheets, and exhibits simultaneously. We hope these advancements will make high-quality technical reviews more widely accessible for knowledge workers everywhere.

items.title: NVIDIA VFX Nodes 登陆 ComfyUI，支持视频超分、补帧与 SDR 转 HDR
items.title_en: Nvidia VFX Nodes for Video Upscaling, Frame Generation and SDR-to-HDR, for VFX Professionals
items.summary: NVIDIA 的 RTX 视频特效现以自定义节点形式在 ComfyUI 中本地运行，官方推荐按超分、补帧、HDR 的顺序搭建完整 VFX 管线。
items.fullContent:
Releasing Nvidia VFX Nodes for Video Upscaling, Frame Generation and SDR-to-HDR, for VFX Professionals
ComfyUI Newsletter
Subscribe Sign in
Nvidia VFX Nodes for Video Upscaling, Frame Generation and SDR-to-HDR, for VFX Professionals
Upscale, interpolate, and convert to HDR locally on your RTX GPU, with better EXR support and color management built for VFX pipelines.
Rob and Alexis Rolland
Oct 13, 2026
7
4
Share
Nvidia’s RTX video effects now run inside ComfyUI as custom nodes . The models are fast, lightweight, ship with the nodes, and run locally on your Nvidia RTX GPU.
Nodes & Models Highlight
The RTX Video Super Resolution node upscales images and video frames up to 4×, either by a multiplier or to target dimensions up to 8192 px. The same node can also denoise or deblur a source without changing its resolution.
The RTX Video Frame Generation node creates new frames between adjacent pairs, for frame-rate conversion or slow motion. It works at 2× to 16× or at a specific timestep.
The RTX Video HDR node converts SDR images to BT.2020 HDR data, with HLG or PQ output. Contrast, saturation, middle gray, and peak luminance from 400 to 2000 nits are all adjustable, and a debanding pass is on by default.
Full workflow, optimal sequence is Super Resolution → Frame Generation → HDR
With the NVIDIA VFX Nodes, you can now run a full professional grade VFX pipeline end-to-end. Chaining the nodes from Video Super Resolution → Frame Generation → Video HDR is a quick and simple way to level up your footage and prepare it for the rest of your VFX pipeline.
The RTX Video Super Resolution node is a great option for efficient upscaling and has 19 modes that can handle different kinds of source material.
Standard modes upscale typical compressed footage.
High-bitrate modes upscale clean or lossless sources without unnecessary artifact suppression.
Streaming modes are tuned for broadcast and webcam streams.
Denoise and deblur modes clean up noise, compression artifacts, or softness and keep the input resolution.
A plain bicubic mode is also available when you don’t need AI processing.
Most modes run from LOW to ULTRA , trading speed for detail. An optional 10-bit encoding preserves more precision. The frame count and frame rate are unchanged, which sets your footage up for the next step in the workflow.
The RTX Video Frame Generation node offers two ways to generate new frames within an input video. Frame-rate multiplier mode fills every gap evenly, from 2× to 16×. To keep the original duration, encode the output at the source frame rate times the multiplier. Specific-timestep mode inserts one frame per pair at any point between the two frames, which suits custom timing in downstream workflows. The Quality parameter runs from LOW, MEDIUM and HIGH . Shot changes are detected automatically, and a manual option marks a known cut. Like RTX Video Super Resolution, the node offers an optional 10-bit encoding for more precision.
In the final step of the workflow, use the RTX Video HDR node to convert SDR images to BT.2020 HDR at their original dimensions. You can tune the conversion with three tone controls. The Contrast and saturation parameters work as they do in any grade. Middle gray sets the reference level for midtones, which decides how bright the overall image sits. Peak luminance tells the node how bright the brightest highlights should get. Set it to match the display you’re grading for, anywhere from 400 to 2000 nits. A debanding pass is on by default, which helps smooth out the visible steps that can show up in gradients like skies when SDR footage is stretched to a wider range. The output is a standard ComfyUI image with no color-space metadata, so downstream Create Video nodes need to be told whether the data is HDR or HDR PQ. The color management and EXR support in this release also handle that step.
Finally, the node pack’s example_workflows folder has a starter workflow for each node: image upscaling, video upscaling, frame generation, and HDR conversion, plus one for converting longer videos to HDR using the loop nodes. To see all three nodes working together, try the full VFX pipeline below.
Nvidia VFX Nodes Workflow
Better EXR support for VFX pipelines
In addition to Nvidia’s VFX nodes, we’re improving support for EXR files format. EXR is the standard format in VFX pipelines, and this release makes it much easier to work with in ComfyUI.
The Save Image (Advanced) node can now write half-float (16-bit) EXRs, now the default, as well as full-float (32-bit) EXRs.
The Load Image node has been improved to ensure images remain intact. It now reads half-float and full-float EXRs. Superwhites above 1.0 and negative values come through untouched instead of being silently clipped, so the full range of data is preserved.
Color management gets an upgrade as well. The Convert Image Color Space node handles sRGB, scene-linear Rec.709, HDR HLG and PQ (Rec.2020), ARRI LogC3 (EI 800) and ACEScct.
Convert Image Color Space node, EXR preview in Load Image and Save Image (Advanced) nodes.
Preview & Download EXRs
EXRs also get a major quality-of-life improvement: they are now easier to inspect and to download. Since web browsers can’t display EXR files, our new asset management system attaches a JPEG preview to every EXR output. The preview is visible in the save and load nodes, in the Assets panel, and in the Jobs history. The small sun button in the load and save nodes also opens the EXR file in the HDR Viewer for more comfortable viewing.
Remark: Previews are only available when ComfyUI starts with the command line argument --enable-asset . The flag is set by default in Comfy Desktop since version 1.1.7 and in ComfyUI portable since 0.40.0 .
Finally, when a save node outputs a sequence of images, the new Download images action lets you pick frames, or hit “Download all”, and download them as a single zip.
Getting Started
Update ComfyUI to the latest version.
Install the Nvidia VFX custom nodes from the ComfyUI Manager.
Load the example workflows from the custom nodes templates, or download the workflows here .
Try it on Comfy Cloud , and let us know what you make. As always, enjoy creating!
